title: Tsongkhapa
hook: the founder of the Gelug school: renunciation, bodhicitta, right view

segments.voice: Yesterday, Longchenpa, and the mind's natural state, clear water when the stirring stops. When did you set your mind down like a glass? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

Here's a hard question for a slow evening. Out of everything you've ever been taught, if you could keep only three things, which would they be? Not three facts. Three things that hold the rest together. A Tibetan monk once answered that question for the whole Buddhist path. He wrote a long, careful book on the stages of the way to awakening. He also wrote a short poem that boils it down to three. Today, Tsongkhapa.
screen: `KEEP ONLY THREE THINGS.` → `A LONG BOOK ON THE PATH.` → `AND A SHORT POEM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Tsongkhapa is remembered as the founder of the Gelug school. Tradition says he studied with teachers from several Tibetan lineages, prized monastic discipline and careful reasoning, and wrote the Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path. His short poem is called the Three Principal Aspects of the Path, and tradition says he wrote it as a letter to a student far away. Second, renunciation. Not throwing everything away, but a clear decision to be free: seeing that chasing one more comfort never ends the restlessness, and turning toward something steadier. Third, bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings. The poem's logic is plain. Renunciation alone could become a private escape. Bodhicitta turns the journey outward, so the freedom sought is freedom for everyone, your neighbors included. Fourth, right view: understanding emptiness, that things arise in dependence on causes and do not stand on their own. Without it, the poem says, even renunciation and bodhicitta cannot cut the root of suffering. Put it in everyday terms. A traveler needs a reason to leave home, someone to make the trip for, and a true map. Leave out any one and the journey stalls. In the Gelug school, students learn this short text and come back to it, the long book folded into a pocket.
screen: `A LONG BOOK, AND A LETTER-POEM.` · `RENUNCIATION: DECIDING TO BE FREE.` · `BODHICITTA: FREEDOM FOR EVERYONE.` · `RIGHT VIEW: NOTHING STANDS ALONE.` · then, large: `A REASON, A PERSON, A MAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your three principal things. Settle, and give the breath a few slow rounds. Ask, quietly, what you want to be free of. Not a list, just one honest answer. Rest with it. Then ask who you'd want that freedom for, besides yourself. Let a face or two appear. Then ask what you'd need to see clearly for any of it to work. Let the answer be simple, even unfinished. Three questions, three short answers. You don't have to use Tsongkhapa's words. Notice what yours are. The bell holds the time.
Tsongkhapa. The founder of the Gelug school, who folded the whole path into three principal aspects: renunciation, bodhicitta and right view. Today's word.
Your line: three principal things. Today, before one real choice, run it past all three: what it frees you from, who else it serves, and whether you're seeing it clearly. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Students in the Gelug school recite Tsongkhapa's Three Principal Aspects of the Path, hear it taught by their teachers, and study his Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path as a map of the whole way.

fork.setup: a student says, "I've decided to be free. that's all I need, isn't it?" you're Tsongkhapa. what's missing?
options: the wish to awaken for everyone, and right view
fork.reveal: in the poem, renunciation alone can become a private escape; bodhicitta and right view complete the path.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: the mind set on awakening for the sake of all beings, the second of the three.

trapdoor: what you thought: three good habits for a calmer life.
what it means: renunciation, bodhicitta and right view, the whole Buddhist path in three principal aspects.
what a scholar hears: the short Three Principal Aspects is read in the Gelug school as a summary of Tsongkhapa's Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path.

notes: Editor: removed the implied order (long book first, 'then' the poem) that the sources don't state; softened 'Gelug students memorize' to a non-sweeping line; changed the carry, which repeated day 968's 'write your three steps on paper'.
No public-domain translation on the validator's list; Tsongkhapa's poem is paraphrased throughout.
'Written as a letter to a student far away' is framed as tradition; confirm (often named as Tsakho Ngawang Drakpa).
'Studied with teachers from several Tibetan lineages': general; confirm.
The poem's claim that without right view, renunciation and bodhicitta cannot cut the root of samsara: paraphrased; confirm.
'Gelug students memorize this short text': general; confirm or soften.
The traveler image (reason, person, map) is an illustration, not from the text.
Audit: 'the freedom you want' told the listener what they want; now 'the freedom sought'.
